```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) {
  knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
}
options(poolinfo.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
# Bounds in the text are rounded outward, so that they stay true.
up <- function(x, digits = 2) num(ceiling(x * 10^digits - 1e-9) / 10^digits, digits)
down <- function(x, digits = 2) num(floor(x * 10^digits + 1e-9) / 10^digits, digits)
pct <- function(x) round(100 * x)
has_metafor <- requireNamespace("metafor", quietly = TRUE)
```

Small area estimation often starts from a survey that gives a direct
estimate for each area, such as a district or a county, with a variance
computed from the survey design. In the area-level model of @fay1979,
the direct estimates play the part of a multisite trial's site estimates.
Each direct estimate is normal around the area's true value, with its
sampling variance $v_j$, and the true values are normal around a
regression on area covariates, with variance $\sigma_\tau^2$. Under this
model, the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) of an area's true value
pulls the direct estimate toward the regression prediction and keeps the
weight

$$
S_j = \frac{\sigma_\tau^2}{\sigma_\tau^2 + v_j}
$$

on the area's own estimate. These weights are poolinfo's site
reliabilities. In this vignette we compute their diagnostics for a set of
simulated areas under two mean models, and we set the posterior means
beside the empirical BLUP (EBLUP). We report the informativeness $I$, the
mean reliability $\bar S$, the dispersion $H$, the logit variance $V$ and
the concentration count $J_{\mathrm{eff}}$ of each fit, as
`vignette("poolinfo")` defines them.

In the small area literature the same quantities go by other letters.
Much of the Fay-Herriot literature writes $A$ for $\sigma_\tau^2$ and
$D_j$ for $v_j$, and @rao2015 write

- $\sigma_v^2$ for $\sigma_\tau^2$, the variance of the true values around
  the regression;
- $\psi_j$ for $v_j$, the sampling variance of area $j$'s direct estimate;
- $\gamma_j$ for $S_j$, the weight on the area's direct estimate.

```{r library}
library(poolinfo)
```

## Simulated areas

We simulate areas whose survey samples differ widely in size. Each direct
estimate is a mean, with a design effect of 1.5 on its variance, and the
true area means depend on a covariate `x`, such as a standardized measure
of poverty from administrative records.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(20261014)
J <- 150
n <- pmax(8, round(exp(rnorm(J, log(60), 0.9))))
x <- rnorm(J)
truth <- 0.2 + 0.4 * x + rnorm(J, sd = 0.15)
se <- sqrt(1.5 / n)
areas <- data.frame(area = sprintf("A%03d", seq_len(J)), n = n, x = x,
                    estimate = rnorm(J, truth, se), se = se)
summary(areas$n)
```

```{r simulate-facts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(min(areas$n) >= 8, max(areas$n) > 300)
```

Across the `r J` areas, samples range from `r min(areas$n)` to
`r max(areas$n)` respondents, with a median of `r median(areas$n)`. In a
real application, `estimate` and `se` would be each area's direct estimate
and its design-based standard error. Like the analysis of a multisite
trial, the Fay-Herriot model treats the sampling variances as known,
although they are estimated from the same small samples. In practice the
direct variances are often smoothed first, for example with a generalized
variance function, before they enter the model [@rao2015]. Whatever noise
the variances carry passes into the diagnostics. $V$ is the variance of
the logarithms of the $v_j$, so independent errors in the estimated
variances tend to raise it, and they spread the reliabilities further
apart. Our simulation uses the true variances, which stand in for
smoothed ones.

## A common mean and a regression mean

We fit the posterior twice, first with a common mean for all the areas
and then with the covariate in the mean, as in the Fay-Herriot model.
`mean_model` takes a one-sided formula, and its variables are looked up in
`data`.

```{r fits}
common <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, site = area, data = areas)
regression <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, site = area,
                                    data = areas, mean_model = ~ x)
compare_profiles(`common mean` = common, `mean model ~ x` = regression)
```

```{r fit-facts, include = FALSE}
pc <- profile_summary(common)
pr <- profile_summary(regression)
get <- function(ps, q, col = "mean") ps[[col]][ps$quantity == q]
stopifnot(get(pc, "I") > 0.85, get(pr, "I") < 0.6,
          get(pr, "sigma_tau") < get(pc, "sigma_tau") / 2,
          abs(get(pc, "V") - get(pr, "V")) < 1e-12,
          get(pr, "H") > 2 * get(pc, "H"),
          abs(get(pr, "I") - 0.5) < abs(get(pc, "I") - 0.5))
```

With a common mean, the between-area standard deviation includes
everything that the covariate explains. Its posterior mean is
`r num(get(pc, "sigma_tau"), 3)` and $I$ is `r num(get(pc, "I"))`, so the
model would move an area with the geometric-mean standard error only about
`r pct(1 - get(pc, "I"))`% of the way toward the common mean. With the
covariate, $\sigma_\tau$ is the standard deviation of the true values
around the regression line,
`r num(get(pr, "sigma_tau"), 3)`, and $I$ falls to `r num(get(pr, "I"))`.
Because the Fay-Herriot predictor shrinks toward the regression
prediction, the second profile is the one that describes it. When you
report the diagnostics of an area-level model, report them for the mean
model that your predictor uses.

Both fits have the same logit variance, $V = `r num(get(pr, "V"))`$,
because $V$ depends on the standard errors alone. Their dispersions differ
(`r num(get(pc, "H"), 3)` with the common mean and
`r num(get(pr, "H"), 3)` with the covariate), because the leading term of
$H$, $I(1 - I)V/2$, is largest at $I = 1/2$.

We print the fit with the covariate, which lists the posterior of the
regression coefficients beside the diagnostics.

```{r regression}
regression
```

```{r regression-facts, include = FALSE}
coef_mean <- function(name) get(pr, paste0("coef_", name))
stopifnot(all(regression$checks$status == "ok"))
```

Its intercept and slope have posterior means of
`r num(coef_mean("(Intercept)"), 3)` and `r num(coef_mean("x"), 3)`. Each
area counts once in the diagnostics, whether its sample has `r min(areas$n)`
respondents or `r max(areas$n)`.

## Concentration of the reliability

A direct estimate's variance here is proportional to $1/n$, so the
`r round(max(areas$n) / min(areas$n))`-fold range of the sample sizes
carries over to the variances. `plot_concentration()` shows how the total
reliability $\sum_j S_j$ accumulates over the areas, from the most reliable
one down.

```{r concentration, fig.alt = "The cumulative proportion of the total reliability against the fraction of areas, most reliable first, for the model with the covariate, with the diagonal of equal proportions."}
plot_concentration(regression, label_top = 0)
```

```{r concentration-facts, include = FALSE}
sites <- site_table(regression)
q <- sort(sites$share, decreasing = TRUE)
top_quarter <- sum(q[seq_len(J / 4)])
precision <- sort(1 / areas$se^2, decreasing = TRUE)
top_precision <- sum(precision[seq_len(J / 4)]) / sum(precision)
stopifnot(top_quarter > 0.3, top_quarter < 0.45,
          top_precision > top_quarter + 0.1, max(sites$reliability) < 0.95)
```

At a quarter of the areas the curve reaches `r pct(top_quarter)`%, so the
most reliable quarter carries that proportion of the total reliability,
although it has `r pct(top_precision)`% of the total precision, the sum of
the $1/v_j$. A reliability cannot exceed 1, and the most precise areas,
with reliabilities up to `r num(max(sites$reliability))`, cannot carry
reliability in proportion to their precision. So the total reliability
is spread more evenly over the areas than the precision is, and the
concentration count of `r num(get(pr, "J_eff"), 1)` of `r J` puts that
spread in one number.

## The areas

We plot each direct estimate beside the posterior mean of its area's true
value, with the areas ordered by reliability. With this many areas the
plot has no labels, and we name its horizontal axis after what it shows.

```{r pooling, fig.height = 6, message = FALSE, fig.alt = "The direct estimates of 150 areas with their 95% intervals, beside the posterior means of the area values with their 95% posterior intervals, ordered by reliability from the least reliable area at the bottom."}
plot_pooling(regression, order = "reliability") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Area mean")
```

```{r pooling-facts, include = FALSE}
least <- which.min(sites$reliability)
most <- which.max(sites$reliability)
width_ratio <- function(i) {
  (sites$effect_upper[i] - sites$effect_lower[i]) / (2 * 1.96 * sites$se[i])
}
stopifnot(width_ratio(least) < 0.5, width_ratio(most) > 0.85)
```

The least reliable areas are at the bottom. Their posterior intervals are
much shorter than the intervals of their direct estimates (for the least
reliable area, `r pct(width_ratio(least))`% as long), and their posterior
means lie away from the direct estimates, toward the regression
predictions. Toward the top the two intervals of an area nearly coincide,
and for the most reliable area the posterior interval is
`r pct(width_ratio(most))`% as long as the direct one.

`site_table()` gives the numbers behind the plot. We add each area's
regression prediction, the intercept plus the slope times `x` at their
posterior means, and show the three areas with the smallest standard
errors and the three with the largest.

```{r table}
coefs <- subset(profile_summary(regression), grepl("^coef_", quantity))$mean
tab <- site_table(regression)
tab$prediction <- coefs[1] + coefs[2] * areas$x
tab <- tab[order(tab$se), c("site", "estimate", "prediction", "se",
                            "reliability", "effect")]
print(rbind(head(tab, 3), tail(tab, 3)), digits = 2)
```

```{r table-facts, include = FALSE}
moved <- (tab$effect - tab$estimate) / (tab$prediction - tab$estimate)
stopifnot(tab$reliability[1] > 0.85, tab$reliability[nrow(tab)] < 0.2,
          all(moved > 0 & moved < 1),
          max(abs(moved - (1 - tab$reliability))) < 0.05)
```

Each posterior mean lies between the area's direct estimate and its
prediction, about $1 - S_j$ of the way from the first to the second. In
the first three rows, with reliabilities of
`r down(min(head(tab$reliability, 3)))` and more, the posterior means stay
near the direct estimates. In the last three, with reliabilities of
`r up(max(tail(tab$reliability, 3)))` or less, they move most of the way
to the predictions.

## Posterior means and the EBLUP

The posterior means here come from the normal model with flat priors on
the coefficients and on $\sigma_\tau$, averaged over the posterior of
$\sigma_\tau$. In the usual Fay-Herriot predictor, the EBLUP, an estimate
of $\sigma_\tau^2$ such as the REML estimate goes into the BLUP instead
[@rao2015]. metafor fits the same model by REML. Next we compute the
profile at its estimate, and the largest difference between an EBLUP, from
`metafor::blup()`, and the posterior mean of the same area.

```{r eblup, eval = has_metafor}
fh <- metafor::rma(estimate, sei = se, mods = ~ x, data = areas,
                   method = "REML")
reliability_profile(fh)
max(abs(metafor::blup(fh)$pred - site_table(regression)$effect))
```

```{r eblup-facts, include = FALSE, eval = has_metafor}
I_reml <- reliability_profile(fh)$stats[["I"]]
gap <- plugin_gap(regression)
I_at_mean <- gap$at_mean_sigma2[gap$functional == "I"]
eblup_diff <- max(abs(metafor::blup(fh)$pred - sites$effect))
I_spread <- diff(range(c(I_reml, I_at_mean, get(pr, "I"))))
stopifnot(I_spread < 0.01, eblup_diff < 0.01)
```

`r if (has_metafor) sprintf("At the REML estimate, $\\sigma_\\tau = %s$ and $I = %s$, against a posterior mean of %s for $I$ and a value of %s at the posterior mean of $\\sigma_\\tau^2$. With %d areas the 95%% posterior interval of $\\sigma_\\tau$ runs from %s to %s, so these three values of $I$ lie within %s of one another, and no EBLUP differs from its area's posterior mean by more than %s.", num(sqrt(fh$tau2), 3), num(I_reml, 3), num(get(pr, "I"), 3), num(I_at_mean, 3), J, num(get(pr, "sigma_tau", "lower"), 3), num(get(pr, "sigma_tau", "upper"), 3), up(I_spread, 3), up(eblup_diff, 3))`
With few areas the posterior mean of $I$, its value at the posterior mean
of $\sigma_\tau^2$ and its value at the REML estimate can be far apart, as
`vignette("posterior-summaries")` shows for the eight schools.
